Cruise Scam UK: How to Spot Fake Holiday Deals and Protect Your Money

Cruise scammers use fake websites, emails, and social media ads to trap UK travellers into paying for holidays that don't exist.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-11 · 8 min read

cruise scam UKfake cruise bookingcruise holiday scamtravel scam UKfake cruise operator
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

What cruise scams look like

Cruise scams come in several forms, but they all aim to steal money or personal data before you realise the booking is fake. The most common version is a fake website or email that mimics a real cruise operator or travel agent, offering heavily discounted cruises to destinations like the Mediterranean, Caribbean, or Norwegian fjords. You may be contacted via email, social media, text message, or a pop-up ad with an offer that seems too good to be true—often 40–60% off standard prices, or a 'last-minute deal' that expires within hours.

The scammer may claim to be clearing inventory, running a promotion, or offering an exclusive member discount. Once you click through or reply, you are directed to a fake booking page where you enter payment details and personal information. The scammer takes your money and disappears, leaving you with no booking, no confirmation, and no way to contact the 'company'. Some variants involve a fake confirmation email that looks authentic, complete with a booking reference and itinerary, to make you believe the transaction is real.

Warning signs of a fake cruise offer

  • **Unsolicited contact with an unbeatable price.** Legitimate cruise operators do not cold-contact you via email or social media with 50% discounts. If you did not search for the deal yourself, be very suspicious.
  • **Pressure to pay immediately.** Scammers use urgency ('offer expires in 2 hours', 'only 3 cabins left') to stop you thinking clearly. Real cruise lines allow time to review terms and payment plans.
  • **A website URL that is slightly wrong.** Check the domain carefully: fake sites may use 'cruises-uk.com' instead of the real operator's official domain, or hide the real name in a longer URL.
  • **Poor spelling, grammar, or design.** Many fake cruise websites have clumsy layouts, broken images, or obvious typos. Real cruise operators invest in professional websites.
  • **No phone number or a number that does not match the official company.** Scam sites often have no contact details, or a generic number that does not connect to the real cruise line.
  • **Payment by bank transfer, gift card, or cryptocurrency only.** Legitimate travel companies accept credit cards and debit cards, which offer buyer protection. Scammers push methods that cannot be reversed.
  • **A booking confirmation that arrives instantly or within minutes.** Real cruise bookings take time to process and confirm. An instant email is a red flag.
  • **The offer came from a social media ad or message, not the official website.** Scammers run fake ads on Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok. Always go directly to the cruise operator's official website instead.

How the scam unfolds from first contact to payment

The scam typically begins with an email, social media message, or pop-up ad offering a discounted cruise. The message includes a link to what looks like a real booking website—often a near-perfect copy of a genuine cruise operator's site, with the same logos, colours, and layout. You click the link and browse cabins and itineraries, which all appear legitimate. When you select a cruise and proceed to checkout, you are asked to enter your full name, address, email, phone number, and payment details.

The fake website may also ask for your passport number or date of birth to 'verify' your booking. You enter your credit or debit card details (or are asked to pay by bank transfer), and the page confirms your booking with a reference number and a fake confirmation email. At this point, the scammer has your money and your personal data. Days or weeks later, when you try to check in online or contact the cruise operator to confirm your booking, you discover the booking does not exist.

The email address you used to book is no longer active, the website has disappeared or changed, and the cruise line has no record of your payment. By then, the scammer has either spent your money or sold your personal details to other criminals.

How to verify a cruise booking is genuine

Before you pay for any cruise, take these steps to confirm it is real. First, do not click any link in an email or social media message. Instead, go directly to the cruise operator's official website by typing the company name into Google and clicking the verified result (look for a blue tick or 'official website' label). Once on the real website, log in to your account or search for the cruise you were offered. If the deal does not appear on the official site, it is fake.

Second, call the cruise operator directly using the phone number on their official website or on your bank card—never use a number from the email or ad. Ask them to confirm whether the price and offer are genuine. Third, check the website URL carefully: it should match exactly what you see on official marketing materials and your bank statements. Fourth, if you have already entered payment details on a suspicious site, contact your bank immediately on the number on the back of your card and ask them to cancel the transaction and monitor your account for fraud.

You can also report the fake website to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk if it arrived by email.

What to do if you have already paid for a fake cruise

Act quickly. First, contact your bank or card issuer on the number on the back of your card (or call 159 to reach your bank's fraud team). Tell them you believe you have been scammed and ask them to cancel the transaction if it has not yet cleared, or to start a chargeback if the money has already left your account. A chargeback is a formal dispute that may recover your money, but you must report it within a set timeframe—usually 120 days.

Second, change your passwords for any online accounts you use, especially email and banking apps, because the scammer now has your personal details and may try to access your accounts. If you gave your passport number or date of birth, monitor your credit file using a free service like Clearscore or Experian to watch for fraudulent applications in your name. Third, report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or online at reportfraud.org.uk. This helps the police and fraud teams track the scammer.

Fourth, report the fake website or email to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk if it was phishing, or forward any scam text messages to 7726. Finally, contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 if you need help understanding your rights or next steps.

Reporting cruise scams in the UK

Report the scam through multiple channels to maximise the chance of action. Start with Report Fraud (0300 123 2040 or reportfraud.org.uk), which is the official UK fraud reporting service run by the National Fraud Intelligence Bureau. They will log your report and may investigate if the scam is part of a larger operation. If the scam arrived by email, forward it to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk—they work to take down phishing websites and can act quickly. If you received a text message, forward it to 7726 (free from any UK mobile).

Report the fake website to the cruise operator themselves by contacting their official customer service team—they can report it to their web hosting provider and help warn other customers. You can also report the scam to Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133, who can advise you on consumer rights and may escalate the case if it is part of a pattern. If the scam involved a social media ad or message, report it directly to the platform (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, etc.) using their 'report' or 'spam' button. Keep copies of all emails, screenshots, and transaction records to share with investigators.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if a cruise website is real or fake?

Go directly to the cruise operator's official website by typing their name into Google—do not click links from emails or ads. Check the URL matches exactly (e.g., 'royalcaribbean.com', not 'royal-caribbean-deals.com'). Call the cruise line on the number from their official website or your bank card to confirm the price and offer. If the deal does not appear on their real website, it is fake.

I paid for a cruise on a website that now looks suspicious. What should I do?

Contact your bank immediately on the number on the back of your card (or call 159) and tell them you may have been scammed. Ask them to cancel the transaction or start a chargeback. Change your passwords for email and banking. Report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040) and the NCSC (report@phishing.gov.uk). Monitor your credit file for fraudulent activity.

Can I get my money back if I paid a cruise scammer?

If you paid by credit or debit card, your bank can start a chargeback, which is a formal dispute that may recover your money—but you must report it within 120 days. If you paid by bank transfer or gift card, recovery is much harder and less likely. Report the scam to Report Fraud and your bank as soon as possible to improve your chances.

What should I do if I received a scam cruise email or text?

Do not click any links. If it arrived by email, forward it to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. If it was a text message, forward it to 7726 (free). Delete the message and report it to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040). If you clicked the link but did not pay, monitor your bank account and credit file for suspicious activity.

Is it safe to book a cruise through a travel agent or comparison website?

Yes, if the travel agent or website is well-known and legitimate. Use established UK travel agents or comparison sites you recognise. Always check the website URL carefully and call the cruise operator directly to confirm the price before paying. Avoid booking through unsolicited emails, social media ads, or unknown websites, even if the price seems very good.
